intro: The delivery is a kinetic chain. Force comes up from the ground through the legs and pelvis, gets amplified by the trunk, and is released through the arm. Each phase asks specific joints for specific range, and loads specific tissues. Values are typical of adult (college and pro) pitchers in lab studies. They vary by pitcher, pitch type and measurement method.

phases.name: Wind-up
phases.span: First movement → lead knee at its highest (balance point)
phases.summary: The pitcher loads onto the drive leg and lifts the lead leg. Little force is made here. The job is a stable, repeatable starting position over the rubber.

positions.value: Self-selected; height varies widely and does not predict velocity on its own

muscles.name: Drive-leg glutes, quadriceps, foot intrinsics
muscles.role: Single-leg balance (isometric)

muscles.name: Lead-leg hip flexors
muscles.role: Lift the knee (concentric)

muscles.name: Trunk stabilizers
muscles.role: Keep posture over the drive leg

muscles.name: Shoulder muscles
muscles.role: Low activity (<25% of max)

phases.tissue: Very low. Problems here show up later as timing faults, not as tissue overload.
phases.sc: Single-leg balance and hip control on the drive side. Screen with single-leg squat and balance holds; this is where control deficits first become visible.
phases.watch: Drifting toward the plate early, or collapsing the drive knee.

phases.name: Stride
phases.summary: The drive leg pushes the body toward the plate while the pelvis stays mostly closed. The hands separate and the throwing arm rises. At foot contact the pelvis starts to open while the upper trunk stays closed, creating hip-shoulder separation.

positions.measure: Lead knee flexion at foot contact

positions.value: ≈40–60° at or just after foot contact (approximate, lab-dependent)

muscles.name: Drive-leg glute max, hamstrings, adductors
muscles.role: Push toward the plate (concentric)

muscles.name: Lead-leg adductors
muscles.role: Control stride width and landing (eccentric)

muscles.name: Deltoid, supraspinatus, upper trapezius
muscles.role: Raise the throwing arm (moderate activity)

muscles.name: Serratus anterior, trapezius
muscles.role: Upwardly rotate the scapula

phases.tissue: Lead-leg adductors and groin on landing. Drive-hip flexors at full extension.

rom.why: Keeping the trunk closed while the pelvis opens

phases.sc: Lateral and rotational power from the drive leg (lateral bounds, heidens, rotational med-ball throws). Adductor strength for landing: test with the squeeze test.
phases.watch: Opening the trunk early (no separation). It shifts load onto the arm in the next phase.

phases.name: Arm cocking
phases.span: Lead foot contact → maximal shoulder external rotation (MER)
phases.summary: The lead leg plants, the pelvis then trunk rotate toward the plate, and the arm lags behind into extreme external rotation (layback). The elbow and shoulder are stretched like a spring. Peak elbow valgus load happens here.

positions.value: ≈170–180°, a composite of GH ER, scapular posterior tilt and trunk extension

muscles.name: Subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi
muscles.role: Brake ER at end range (eccentric), then start IR

muscles.name: Infraspinatus, teres minor, supraspinatus
muscles.role: Center the humeral head (compression)

muscles.name: Serratus anterior
muscles.role: Hold the scapula (high activity)

muscles.name: Biceps, flexor-pronator mass
muscles.role: Stabilize the elbow; flexor-pronator resists valgus dynamically

muscles.name: Lead-leg quadriceps
muscles.role: Firm the front leg (eccentric to isometric)

muscles.name: Obliques
muscles.role: Rotate the trunk toward the plate

phases.tissue: UCL (valgus tension), medial elbow and flexor-pronator origin. Lateral elbow compression (radiocapitellar). Anterior capsule. Posterosuperior labrum and undersurface cuff (internal impingement); biceps-labral peel-back (SLAP).

rom.why: Layback; most of the ER gain in throwers is used here
Adds to layback and keeps the glenoid under the head
Lead hip starts rotating over the planted leg

phases.sc: Where velocity and elbow load are both made. Train the lead-leg block, trunk rotation power and scapular control (serratus, lower trap). Respect GH ER: don't stretch away an adaptive ER gain.
phases.watch: Early trunk rotation, a short or collapsing lead leg, and arm lag beyond the pitcher's usual layback. All raise shoulder and elbow load.

phases.name: Arm acceleration
phases.summary: The stored energy releases. The elbow extends and the shoulder rotates internally at the fastest angular velocities recorded in sport. The trunk flexes forward and tilts to the glove side over a firm lead leg.

positions.value: More tilt raised velocity and also shoulder and elbow load in high school pitchers

muscles.name: Subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi
muscles.role: Drive IR (concentric, high activity)

muscles.name: Serratus anterior
muscles.role: Protract the scapula with the arm

muscles.name: Triceps
muscles.role: Elbow extension (mostly a stabilizer; extension is largely whip from proximal segments)

muscles.name: Flexor-pronator mass
muscles.role: Valgus support, wrist flexion and pronation through release

muscles.name: Lead-leg quads and glutes
muscles.role: Lead knee extends, braking the pelvis

phases.tissue: UCL (valgus continues). Posteromedial olecranon (valgus extension overload). Flexor-pronator group.

rom.why: Near-full extension at release; an extension deficit shows up here

phases.sc: Speed here comes from the chain, not from training the arm muscles to be faster. Build lead-leg strength (eccentric quads, glutes), anti-rotation and rotation power, and flexor-pronator endurance.
phases.watch: A soft lead knee (energy leaks), or excessive trunk tilt used to chase velocity.

phases.name: Arm deceleration
phases.span: Ball release → maximal shoulder internal rotation
phases.summary: The arm has to stop. Posterior shoulder muscles and the trunk absorb the remaining energy. Joint forces peak: the shoulder sees a compressive (distraction-resisting) force about body weight.

positions.value: Arm crosses the body as IR finishes

muscles.name: Teres minor, infraspinatus
muscles.role: Decelerate IR and resist distraction (eccentric, high activity)

muscles.name: Posterior deltoid, latissimus dorsi
muscles.role: Decelerate horizontal adduction

muscles.name: Lower trapezius, rhomboids
muscles.role: Control scapular protraction

muscles.name: Biceps, brachialis
muscles.role: Decelerate elbow extension (eccentric)

muscles.name: Trunk and lead-hip extensors
muscles.role: Absorb energy as the trunk flexes over the front leg

phases.tissue: Posterior cuff and posterior capsule (eccentric overload, later stiffness and IR loss). Biceps-labral complex. Olecranon.

rom.why: IR completes; posterior tightness and GIRD develop from repeated deceleration

phases.sc: The most trainable injury-risk phase. Eccentric posterior cuff and lower-trap work, and a full follow-through so the trunk and hips share the braking. Monitor IR and total arc across the season.
phases.watch: A short follow-through that makes the arm brake on its own.

phases.name: Follow-through
phases.summary: The body finishes over the lead leg and the remaining energy dissipates. The drive leg swings through and the pitcher recovers to field.

positions.value: Flexed over a stable lead leg

muscles.name: Lead-leg glutes and hamstrings
muscles.role: Hold the trunk over the front leg (eccentric)

muscles.name: Posterior shoulder and scapular muscles
muscles.role: Low to moderate activity as the arm settles

phases.tissue: Low for the arm. Lead hip and lumbar spine take flexion and rotation load.

rom.why: Pelvis finishes rotating over the lead leg

phases.sc: Lead-hip flexion and IR mobility plus eccentric hamstring and glute strength let the trunk finish over the front leg.
phases.watch: Falling off toward first base (right-handed pitcher), a sign of limited lead-hip rotation or a weak block.
